Deep learning models have been successfully trained on static datasets through supervised learning, but they are limited to environments that do not change over time. In contrast, datasets with a large scale are typically collected over extended periods, effectively subject to a dynamic and time-variable unsupervised learning process. Our research investigates whether and how the gathering dataset collection process can be considered a dynamic unsupervised learning process. We developed a system that performs continuous, unsupervised learning on a massive image dataset without requiring labels. By doing so, we can capture the evolving structure of the data and how it changes over time. Our system learned a DNN model that represents a snapshot of the dataset at any given point in time. When the dataset is divided into smaller batches, our model can represent each batch with high accuracy. When compared to a static DNN trained on the entire dataset, our system achieves comparable results. Moreover, it outperforms other one-shot learning models when it comes to categorizing images from different time periods. Our system also ranks the different categories based on their likelihood and these rankings reflect the dataset's evolving structure. By visualizing the top categories and their respective frequencies, we can gain insights into how the data changes over time.

This study discloses novel analytical and geometrical aspects of the generalized algebraic multiplicity $\chi$ already discussed in previous work. We refine a key formula for $\chi$ found in that research and discloses its connection to the standard algebraic multiplicity. We also discodos key relationships between $\chi$ and the geometric multiplicity, as well as $\chi$'s properties under direct sum and inertia transformations. These concepts are further explored using concrete examples.

A novel approach has been proposed for estimating the optical phase in dipole systems, taking into account a unique feature of such a setup - its ability to maintain coherence. This method involves creating bosonic pairs in a matter-field system and leveraging their correlations for optimal phase assessment through a two-step process. First, an optical pulse interacts with the dipole system to transfer the optical phase to the dipole. Next, a cavity interaction with the system generates squeezing between the dipole and the cavity field. It is demonstrated that combining this method with prior research on using pair-created fields for phase assessment results in a significant improvement in sensitivity, surpassing the sensitivity limits of similar methods by a factor of two.

Researchers have developed a novel approach to create a qutrit, an information unit spanning three quantum states, by placing three silicon donor atoms in close proximity and taking into account the electron distribution across different valleys. A precise and efficient computational method based on a donor multi-valley mass operator has been employed to analyze a broad spectrum of electron configurations and locations. This研究 is particularly useful in scenarios where the number of electrons and their corresponding ground-state arrangements is not obvious, and it overlooks complex interactions between hills that typically hinder such processes. Furthermore, it can be applied to cases involving electrons located in separate valleys, a situation frequently encountered in operational quantum circuits and that is often poorly understood. Notably, when two electrons are confined to a single valley, a qutrit composed of three adjacent silicon donor states has been found to exhibit greater resistance to errors caused by environmental noise when compared to a qutrit formed by three donor states within the same zero-valley.

Researchers investigated the quantum conduction of electrons in Dirac particles within HgTe gapless quantum wells, specifically those without an energy gap. Our analysis indicates that in large samples, only the Drude conduction persists, while backscattering of electrons is infinite and prevents the quantum Hall effect from occurring. This outcome is consistent with prior observations, where large samples did not exhibit the quantum Hall effect. Furthermore, our study reveals that a precise relationship between sample size and time exists, where the quantum Hall effect can occur in smaller samples but not in larger ones, all without an energy gap or opening one, theoretically.

Nominal orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) has been widely adopted in 5G systems due to its scalability, yet it suffers from impaired security as users are dynamically paired. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel, intersection-based collaborative NOMA (ICN) protocol for road intersections, where security is prioritized. In this protocol, vehicle-to-vehicle links are substituted with reliable infrastructure-to-vehicle connections, allowing for persistent user pairing. Through theoretical analysis and simulations, we evaluate the performance of ICN protocol under extreme conditions. When compared to traditional dynamic NOMA (DNOMA), the ICN protocol offers enhanced average throughputs of up to 100% and 250% for low and high traffic loads, respectively, while providing 100% sum-throughputs gains over static NOMA (SNOMA) across all scenarios.

This paper presents an innovative solution to manage Dynamic Time Division Duplexing (TDD) in 5G networks, which offer higher spectral efficiency but suffer from potential uplink/downlink interference due to neighboring cells operating on different frequencies at different times. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel scheduling method for uplink and downlink slots in D-TDD systems by incorporating a stochastic game-theoretic framework that accounts for the probabilistic nature of cell neighbors' TDD configurations. Our approach ensures the stability of system operations and provides an optimal schedule to maximize total cell throughput. In a simulated environment, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in achieving high network throughput and provide a way to control the level of interference between cells.

The nonlocal resistance data of BSCCO samples, with a thickness ranging from 10 to 100 nanometers, exhibits a distinct peak at specific magnetic field strengths that indicates the Hall effect. The peak's position aligns with predictions made by the quantum phase slip model, assuming that vortex lines are confined within a one-dimensional space. The expected behavior of the Landau level and the filled vortex lattice's Hall effect do not match the observed effects. By analyzing the disorder in the vortex lattice, taking into account the missing vortices, the predicted behavior matches the observed Hall effect peak. The discrepancy in the expected and observed effects for both large and small samples is further highlighted, and a comparison is made with the effects of disorder in both the Landau level and the filled vortex lattice. The significance of this study is that it provides a clear distinction between the effects of disorder in both systems and confirms the importance of missing vortices in determining the Hall effect.

Researchers have employed the cumulant mapping to analyze the critical behavior of the 3D Ising model, revealing that higher-order cumulants exhibit a second-order phase transition at the critical temperature, with a set of exponents that fall within the Ising range. However, earlier studies indicated that certain odd-order cumulants behaved differently near $T_c$. In this investigation, we have examined higher-order odd-order cumulants, utilizing an expanded fitting approach to Ising exponents. This approach has yielded results showing that some of these cumulants actually follow power laws with Ising exponents at $T_c$. Consequently, our findings suggest that some non-zero fixed points exist within some of the Ising $\epsilon_n$ subuniverses.

We provide a commutative square of inclusions of operator algebras, consisting of a finite-dimensional unitary matrix algebra and a hyperfinite type III factor, with inclusions that are irreducible and equivalent to a single unitary representation, which generates an extensive library of new subfactors that share this representation as their 1-sector. It remains unknown whether there exist finite-dimensional amenable inclusions generating full factors, but we establish a connection to this question. Specifically, if the unitary matrix algebra in our example were substituted with the inclusions of type III factors derived from infinite-dimensional, non-amenable unitary matrices, then the resulting constructed unitary matrix algebra would be a non-amenable unitary matrix algebra.

For effective semi-supervised learning with point clouds, leveraging geometric information from point clouds' inherent structure is crucial. Geometric information can be utilized to create synthetic training data by generating neighboring points through the calculation of implicit curvature values. In this study, a neural network called Hamiltonian Neural Network is employed to derive curvature values from a single input. Subsequently, neighboring points are generated based on the calculated curvature values. Our method leverages this synthetic data to enhance the performance of a semi-supervised learning model. By integrating the synthetic data into the training process, the proposed method yields improved results. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on two public datasets.

Deep learning models that utilize multiple agents have demonstrated remarkable success, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks that can exploit a single vulnerable agent to deceive the rest of the ensemble. Researchers propose a novel framework called Human-ensemble, which combines a multi-agent system with human input to increase confidence in model predictions. This framework employs three types of human-created links between agents: soft connections based on shared tasks, hard connections through model pooling, and virtual hops through information exchange. To demonstrate the effectiveness of Human-ensemble, the developers conducted comprehensive experiments utilizing both real-world and artificial datasets across a range of applications, including image and text classification. The results indicate that Human-ensemble exhibits superior performance compared to single-agent models and standard learning methods, while maintaining interpretability and allowing for insight into the decision-making processes of each agent.

In airport security checkpoints, advanced imaging technology is employed to ensure passenger safety by detecting prohibited items such as weapons and explosives. However, the performance of these systems can be compromised due to difficulties in distinguishing banned objects from regular carry-on items. In response, a new benchmark has been established to assess and enhance the accuracy of prohibited items detection through a novel deep learning approach known as the Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM). This benchmark, which comprises 100,000 data samples and features unique divisions into training, validation, and testing sets, is designed to minimize data bias and ensure reliable evaluation. When compared to the current state-of-the-art methods, a network that incorporates the LIM has demonstrated significant improvements in performance, which have also been further validated through extensive experiments on data with varying levels of noise.

We introduce a new way to describe links in $T^2 \times I$ that uses the path integral method from quantum field theory. This new description is based on the KdV algebra and yields results that are whole numbers. By using certain changes, we can see that our invariant remains consistent and then connect the value of our invariant to the average exponential volume of knots based on the fields in q-deformed geometry.

The issue of word sense discrimination remains unresolved, with no clear solution. Words with multiple meanings, known as polysemes, can be confusing, but the current practice of representing them as context polysemes assumes that their context is always unambiguous, which is not always the case. Moreover, the context of words with a single meaning, or monosemes, is not a focus of study. To address these gaps, this study looks at the context complexity of both polysemes and monosemes, using latent semantic analysis to create the context features of bigram, trigram, and n-gram. By testing a range of context complexity indicators, including singular value decomposition, this study found that the features of context can provide a useful basis for distinguishing between the different senses of a word. When compared to using only word features, or using only decontextualized sense features, incorporating context features significantly improves the accuracy of word sense discrimination, with the best results seen when using trigram features.

A new regularized form of the gamma function is defined through specific expressions involving zeta functions, which can be derived from the standard properties of the gamma function. This definition focuses on expressions that avoid the need for convergence factors in the integral parts of the standard gamma function characteristics. A key expression used to obtain the new definition involves the gamma function in its integral form, combining both discrete and continuous parts of the expression. This work extends the concept of the regularized gamma function to the beta function, which is derived from its standard properties of the gamma function, and the expressions of the regularized gamma function are also related to the half-density of the Riemann surface associated with the exponential function.

The research examines the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions, a process that will be encountered at the future FCC-ee and possible ILC. By analyzing this process through the examination of forward dijet + gamma rates in pp collisions at the LHC, we can predict the outcomes of proton-nucleus collisions. This method involves comparing data with theoretical predictions derived from global parton distribution fits. We specifically evaluate the proton-FoCA fits from PML and nCTEQ15, and investigate the impact of top quark production on global fits by incorporating it with NNLO QCD corrections using APFEL++ and xQCD. The findings indicate an improvement in global fit quality by 0.6-0.9 chi^2 per data point when including these corrections.

Current research on Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL largely centers on individual modules, be it domain mapping, end-2-end parsers or linguistic analysis, but relatively little attention has been given to an often crucial yet under-explored task: SQL parsing. To address this gap, we introduce a unique dataset, MSRA SQL Parse, comprising 10K high-quality parse trees that accurately depict the structural relationship between textual inputs and their corresponding SQL outputs. Building upon the widely used MSRA domain mapping dataset, our novel approach involves introducing two distinct sub-tasks, namely partial-SQL generation and full-SQL generation, and an innovative yet straightforward yet powerful SQL parser, SCParser. SCParser leverages sophisticated textual input encoding, domain mapping, and an attention-based mechanism for hierarchical sequence labeling to learn the structural connection between text and SQL. To further enhance our model, we integrate an end-2-end cross-domain linguistic analysis framework, dubbed MSRA SCParser, comprising high-quality data, two distinct sub-tasks, and our proposed parser. Experimental results demonstrate that MSRA SCParser outperforms existing state-of-the-end Cross-Domain Text-to-SQL parsing models, notably improving overall F1 scores and those of entity and operation level metrics.

The rise of social networking platforms and online services based on connected data has significantly increased our understanding of privacy risks associated with released graphs and development of effective methods for their disclosure. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of research on differential secrecy for graphs, covering a range of approaches and applications while exploring key differential secrecy definitions, measurement techniques, and methods for protecting graph-related data. We discuss key challenges hindering progress in this field and potential areas for future research.

The upcoming mission Euclid will significantly contribute to our understanding of cosmology, offering a comprehensive and high-precision survey of nearly one million precise photometric data points produced by the satellite. This immense resource will present both challenges and possibilities for future research in theoretical and computational physics. A gathering of experts has been convened to explore how to capitalize on the Euclid inheritance science opportunities.

The auto-pilot system for lane keeping is being widely used in new vehicles and its approval for operation is being considered in various countries, which means it will soon be subjected to regulation. To ensure the safety of lane keeping auto-pilot in diverse driving situations, a comprehensive set of test cases is needed. Generating complex path scenarios for testing is a challenging task due to the legal and safety implications of creating realistic traffic conditions. To address this, the goal is to automatically create a set of test scenarios that include intricate paths, diverse traffic conditions, and potentially hazardous situations. This paper proposes a method to efficiently create complex curves and presents an efficient algorithm to connect them smoothly. This, in turn, allows for the automatic creation of complex path scenarios to test the lane keeping auto-pilot system.

Music recommendations are typically provided as a list of individual tracks.
However, offering recommendations at the level of playlists, which can be
viewed as higher-level entities containing multiple songs, has the potential to
be more effective. Achieving this requires creating summaries of music that
capture the mood or genre. This task is relatively new in the field of
automated analysis and currently relies heavily on human input. To advance this
area, we have created a dataset comprising 270k short clips from various genres
and emotions, and developed a ranking-based learning approach to generate
summaries. Our findings indicate that algorithmic music annotation is feasible
and can serve as a valuable tool in developing sophisticated entities like
recommendation systems that rely on music lists.

A new quantum hydrodynamic theory has been developed in the random matrix framework, where the interaction matrix is randomly generated. This new model builds upon previously discovered connections between quantum hydrodynamics and random matrix theory. By applying the corresponding Hartree equation to the interaction matrix's eigenvalues, a quantum hydrodynamic equation of state was derived for a specific interacting system. This derivation was then used to obtain the long-time behavior of a quantum fluid's one-body density matrix. An stochastic hydrodynamic equation was developed for the one-body density matrix, which accounts for an interacting quantum system. This approach was further supported by time-dependent random matrix simulations that demonstrated excellent agreement with both hydrodynamic predictions and exact spectral calculations.

Temporal action localization aims to pinpoint the exact start and end of actions within a video. Most existing methods process the entire video at once, which can be computationally inefficient. In contrast, this work proposes a new framework called DCAN, a temporal action localization method that divides a video into multiple segments and analyzes the context between segments. By breaking the video into manageable parts and analyzing each part and their relationships, DCAN effectively balances global and local context, thus improving accuracy and computational performance.

Recent observations in the JET tokamak have revealed a unique phenomenon known as Palm Tree Modes (PTMs), which have significantly enhanced neoclassical tearing mode stability and led to record-breaking energy densities in some discharges. PTMs were previously unaccounted for in theoretical models due to their intricate structure, characterized by multiple rational surfaces within a single mode structure. A new magnetic perturbation model has now provided a detailed explanation of the PTM structure and its impact on the current profile, showing that PTMs act as localized resonant current islands that may provide greater stabilization than previously thought possible.

This research proposes a safety mechanism for mobile robots that utilizes a mathematical concept called a CVPL, which is a type of landscape similar to vortex potentials but changes over time and is influenced by nearby robots. The proposed CVPL concept is unique due to its ability to identify risks quickly, provide real-time speed information, and offer a clear visualization of potential collisions. A safety protocol is then developed based on the CVPL by selecting actions that minimize the risk of collisions, which can be optimized using a time-based approach and a method known as receding horizon control. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of the CVPL and the safety protocol through various simulations involving multiple robots.

The fundamental concept of information theory, known as Shannon's information theory, relies on the assumption that source terms are statistically independent. However, the nature of human language involves terms that do not exhibit complete independence from one another. This dependence can be represented through directed graphs, where nodes represent terms and edges signify co-occurrence probabilities. Such a model allows for the calculation of a source's entropy based on the statistical data of its terms. A proposed method involves utilizing this approach to quantify the informational content of a source, such as natural language, by measuring the deviation of significant subgroups of term sequences from the assumption of independence.

Recent advancements in wireless communications have incorporated radio frequency reflective surfaces (RRS) to enhance various applications. This technology, however, is not without risks, as malicious actors could manipulate these surfaces to bypass security protocols. Although previous studies have explored attacks on communications utilizing RRS, there has been limited focus on their impact on radar systems. In response, this study introduces a novel concept of smart reflective surfaces (SRS) capable of not manipulating but also optimizing signals reflected, thereby enhancing target parameter estimation in wireless radar systems. A mathematical model is proposed to analyze this concept, and a malicious attack utilizing the reconfigurable surfaces is proposed. Interestingly, the study posits that while an attack can significantly improve target parameter estimation accuracy when targets are closely located, it may have the opposite effect when targets are distant. Furthermore, a comparison between the proposed attack and a conventional method that leverages the SRS to amplify returned signals reveals that in certain scenarios, the proposed approach can yield more precise target parameter estimation.

Dynamic code vulnerability detection through fuzzing has been recognized for its effectiveness. However, existing fuzzer evaluation methods are inadequate, relying on proprietary benchmarks and undisclosed metrics. This study proposes a comprehensive framework for assessing fuzzer performance, including a standardized benchmark collection, clear performance indicators, and a comparison tool. We demonstrate the benefits of this framework by establishing performance benchmarks for state-of-the-art fuzzers, including those based on traditional and advanced techniques. Experiments were conducted on 11 state-of-the-art fuzzers using a diverse set of targets, including C++ libraries, Java programs, and Java bytecode. We found that evaluating a fuzzer's performance should consider multiple aspects, such as coverage generation, vulnerability discovery, and stability. Additionally, we discovered that some highly regarded fuzzers do not consistently outperform others, prompting us to recommend simpler alternatives in certain situations.

In continual learning, the assessment of new models compared to existing ones poses a significant challenge. As a result, recent studies have developed complex evaluation strategies, including contrastive loss functions, to compare models effectively. We challenge this approach by proposing a simple yet effective baseline that utilizes the standard accuracy metric for model comparison. We discover that this baseline outperforms more sophisticated solutions proposed in the field of continual learning across various settings and benchmarks. Our findings suggest that the contrastive loss functions proposed in the field may be over-engineered solutions to an issue that can be solved with our simple baseline approach.

We define a concept called a homotopic minimum region surface for a given metric space X. This surface becomes the point where, for any two points on it that share a specific line segment, the surface has the same outward direction. We demonstrate that a certain type of Dirichlet problem has a solution when the given boundary is a homotopic minimum region surface, and also provide a comparison to a similar concept developed by researchers in a different mathematical field.

This study examines the long-term dynamics of solutions to the heat equation on the real line, subject to a given initial temperature distribution.  Specifically, we investigate scenarios where the temperature distribution approaches a rapidly decaying function as we move in the negative direction and an exponentially increasing function in the opposite direction.  By applying a suitable rescaling technique, we can characterize the temperature distribution at any later time based on the initial conditions.  A key aspect of this research is its unification of previously established results, which focused on situations where the initial temperature distribution either approached a constant or oscillated periodically in one or both directions at the extreme points of the real line.

A strong ground-state proton tensor pairing is observed in an unusual 64Ni nucleus, and experimental data suggest its state exists as a pure 0+ form. This study aims to investigate the unique zero-spin state in 64Ni by implementing a semi-empirical approach that involves adjusting the interaction matrix elements and analyzing the resulting wave function density. A key finding is that a strong ground-state proton tensor pair can exist within 0+ states with specific angular momentum characteristics, and modifying the interaction strength can result in 2p-2h 0+ states transitioning to 0+ ground states, providing an explanation for the observed phenomena in 64Ni.

The stability of correlated equilibria in quantal response equilibrium (QRE) is likely compromised by the sensitivity to utility perturbations, specifically those that adhere to the Lipschitz condition. This sensitivity results in correlated equilibria forming within the strategy space, which ultimately causes the dimensionality of these equilibria sets to be extensive. Our research focuses on establishing lower bounds for the minimum query complexity needed to identify a specific near-optimal component of these equilibria sets. We determine that the minimum query complexity lower bound grows at the rate of the square root of the dimensionality of the equilibria sets, which is directly related to the inverse of the minimum probability of achieving an outcome that meets the criteria. This dimensionality is found to increase as the likelihood of equilibrium outcomes decreases, which in turn increases the minimum query complexity needed to identify a particular high-dimensional correlated equilibrium as the probability of these outcomes approaches zero. This specific issue is examined in greater detail using the example of coordination games featuring numerous potential actions.

A major challenge in developing effective natural language processing models is finding suitable evaluation techniques. Model performance metrics, such as accuracy, are commonly used to assess the efficacy of different approaches. However, inaccuracies in these metrics can mislead researchers about a model's true potential. One significant source of performance estimation error lies in how the data is prepared for training and evaluation. Overfitting, a situation where the model learns to recognize patterns that do not apply to new, unseen data, is often caused by an uneven distribution of labels in the data sets. Studies have shown that even a slight increase in data set size can greatly enhance the accuracy of a prepared data set and, as a result, a model. On the other hand, more complex methods like nested cross-validation are too computationally expensive to use for large-scale processing. We conducted a thorough study to evaluate the effectiveness of various evaluation methods on several types of language processing models and found that K-fold cross-validation with adjusted pairs (J-K) is a suitable method for efficiently assessing a model's performance. We demonstrated that J-K significantly reduces the variance in performance estimates and achieves similar levels of accuracy to more complex methods like nested cross-validation.

This document provides an overview of the distinctive characteristics of educator-pupil and pupil-only learning methods. It then compares and contrasts these two learning frameworks. A comparison of various characteristics of educator-pupil and pupil-only learning methods is also made. We discuss the benefits and drawbacks of educator-pupil learning. In addition, we examine the influence of quality and reliability of instructors on learning outcomes. A comparison of different data visualization techniques used in educator-pupil learning is presented. This survey will serve as a reference point for future research on quality and reliability of instructors and visual representation of knowledge generated through educator-pupil learning.

The expected projection method is a widely recognized and efficient technique for resolving and constraining optimization problems in graphical models, with applications spanning natural language processing, machine reading comprehension, and other areas of AI. Although traditional arithmetic projection methods are fast, they suffer from a significant drawback of being time-consuming when dealing with non-linear functions, which is a common occurrence. This issue is particularly prevalent in the expected marginal posterior mode (MPE) optimization. We address this concern by developing a logarithmic projection method, an expected version of the logarithmic arithmetic projection, and demonstrate its superior performance in expected projections. Our proposed method significantly accelerates the expected projection process, achieving a substantial reduction in computation time, with an average improvement of 10 times over the existing expected arithmetic projection. Furthermore, we extend the logarithmic projection to constrained optimization problems, with an average 5 times speedup overall.

Researchers developed an advanced technique using a single laser to both cool and measure ultracold atoms in a haze of strontium, which was cooled to an exceptionally low temperature of 3 microkelvin. In this process, they found that the laser photons carried more energy when comparing the difference in energy between the start and end points, resulting in a detectable shift in the frequency, amounting to about 16 parts per billion of the total frequency. They found the optimal setup by adjusting the laser's angle, and the difference in the energy amounts to a very narrow range, amounting to about 15 kilohertz. They plan to use this technique to precisely measure changes in the number of strontium atoms and investigate the effects of phase transitions in a particular range of lattice energies.

The sudden shift in viscosity during the shear thickening transition (ST) in concentrated suspensions can be linked to the critical phenomena seen in phase transitions. Researchers believe that near the threshold of the shear thickening transition, mesoscale interactions within the suspension drive this shift. To verify this hypothesis, researchers used ultrasound to visualize the suspension's behavior before and after the ST, both in steady-state and during oscillatory shear. They discovered that a single parameter can describe the scaling of sound speed changes with respect to shear stress, indicating that the critical phenomena exhibited in shear thickening transitions follow a universal pattern.

We establish a connection between the Racah algebra $Rachach(\mathfrak{sl}_2,n)$ and the centralizer $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, revealing the algebraic structure of $Rachach(\mathfrak{sl}_2,n)$ through its generators' degrees. This reveals that $Rachach(\mathfrak{sl}_2,n)$ coincides with the e-normal form of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for all $n\geq 4$. Furthermore, we derive the Hilbert-Poincaré series of $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ for its irreducible components, revealing a pattern that we conjecture holds for all $n\geq 4$.

Our study suggests that in triplon models derived from a double honeycomb Heisenberg antiferromagnet with weak interlayer interactions, fluid phases in the triplon system can undergo a transition to curved supersolid phases, even when there's an excess of triplons. These curved supersolids can be classified into two types: type-A, characterized by local supersolid order within disjoint supersolid regions, and type-B, featuring curved crystals coexisting with triplon fluid in a coexistence pattern. Both types of curved supersolids display unique properties, including the coexistence of supersolid and Mott insulator-like states, and in some cases, type-B curved crystals exhibit incompressibility and inextensibility. Our analysis indicates that the peculiar behavior of these phases can be explained through effective triplon Hamiltonians that incorporate the Dzyaloshinskii-Mololya interaction, and our DREMR analysis shows that the long-range magnetic order exists in the phase diagram's boundary between triplon fluid and curved supersolid regions, specifically at the point where the curvature of the curved crystals reaches its maximum.

This research examines incident and angular recoil speed distributions for WIMP-nucleus scattering, using a direct, non-rigorous method that can be applied to both two and three-dimensional scenarios. In contrast to previous studies, our approach directly calculates the angular recoil speed distribution without relying on the assumption of negligible relative speeds between the WIMP and nucleus. We find that, due to its simplicity, our method yields the same outcomes as those obtained through more complex, rigorous methods. We also find that, for typical WIMP speeds found in the halo model, the relative speed between the WIMP and nucleus is, on average, 1.11 times the relative speed found in the laboratory, indicating a potential need to consider this factor in direct WIMP detection detection rate calculations.

Leveraging Google's Web search as a model, a series of experiments were conducted to measure the amount of relevant information that users may miss due to the algorithm's personalized results. Two types of tasks were used: one requiring the identification of deceptive content and another involving detection of biased opinions. Participants were asked to locate the most impactful advertisement or opinion in a set of randomly selected content, both with and without performing search tasks. Results revealed that while the search process seemed to enhance participants' performance, the actual accuracy was comparable to that of non-search participants. Furthermore, no consistent pattern was observed in which specific content was most frequently identified as the most relevant. These findings suggest that a significant number of useful pieces of information are not reached by the 10 top search results, likely due to the competitive nature of the ranking system.

A novel concept, a Muon-Ion Synchrotron (MIS), has been proposed to potentially overcome limitations associated with conventional synchrotrons and colliders when it comes to exploring specific phenomena, particularly those found beyond the Standard Model. At certain energy levels, the production rates for single photon processes and weak interactions become comparable, which could result in distinctive interactions mediated by W bosons producing heavy neutrinos or leptons, accompanied by significant transverse momentum. However, these processes may suffer from limited data due to their occurrence only once per beam spill. To mitigate this issue, the MIS concept suggests utilizing a high-intensity muon beam coupled with a dense target, such as lead, which could facilitate a wide range of applications, from physics research to novel imaging techniques. Through an initial assessment, we have identified potentially achievable operating parameters for a muon beam with a 10-Tera Watt lead target, which could be further explored through detailed simulations.

Conventional 2D MRI techniques, despite their widespread use in guiding radiation therapy, have certain limitations stemming from their reduced spatial resolution and restricted coverage. A novel MRI sequence has been developed to address these drawbacks, combining highly resolved 2D images over a large scan area with motion correction in real-time. This innovative approach enables efficient, breath-hold 2D scans that maintain their guiding potential while reducing them to a single breath-hold. By utilizing a radial acquisition method, this sequence mitigates the impact of respiratory motion, circumventing the need for prolonged, low-resolution scans. Furthermore, this sequence has been optimized for maximum speed and resolution, resulting in highly precise, minimally distorted images with an effective spatial resolution of approximately 1.25 mm. These images have been demonstrated to be highly suitable for use in forming highly accurate treatment plans for both the head and the body. This sequence has been successfully applied to a broad range of patients, spanning from the head to the thorax and abdomen.

A specific class of nonlinear systems is considered here, including some types of systems that are influenced by adversarial interference. For these systems, a method is developed to design state-based controllers that limit the impact of this interference. This design method is carried out in three stages. Initially, an internal model is used to simplify the effect of interference into a more manageable form. Next, a specialized control barrier function is devised for this modified system to ensure safety. Finally, a feedback controller is developed to limit the impact of any remaining interference that was not fully accounted for by the internal model. This controller also ensures that the system remains stable. Two examples and simulated scenarios are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach.

This study introduces a novel approach to calculating polygon and convex hull areas by utilizing approximation spaces derived from change-finding operators. This method provides a straightforward proof that the areas of a polygon equal the areas of its convex hull, and enables the calculation of complex, non-convex figure areas. An algorithm is proposed to simplify areas by representing them as the sum of rectangular areas, a step crucial for effective area change visualization.

StrucTest was previously introduced as an innovative method for evaluating hypotheses within the context of multiple testing, specifically targeting the use of dependent test statistics. Initially, the proposed method involved a straightforward pairing strategy to enhance the reliability of p-values under 'local independence'. However, this method might not accurately reflect the true independence of individual tests when tests are paired. In this study, we introduce a more sophisticated examination method called the Precise Paired-Permutation (3P) method, which utilizes an advanced permutation technique to better evaluate the reliability of test statistics in complex, structured settings. In contrast to the 3P method, our new approach involves a sophisticated pairing strategy and a precise permutation technique that can better guarantee the validity of test statistics in highly dependent environments. Through both artificial and real-world data sets, including a large-scale study involving nearly 10 million tests, our findings indicate that the Precise Paired-Permutation (3P) method outperforms the original method in terms of accuracy and stability. In contrast to the original method, our new approach involves a sophisticated pairing strategy and a precise permutation technique that can better evaluate the reliability of test statistics in complex, structured settings.

A comprehensive global maritime container freight rate dataset from 1966 to 2016 has been compiled, which has been underutilized by researchers. During the study, sources for acquiring this essential data were identified and demonstrated their reliability. This research also examines various factors that influence freight rates, including shipping rates for other commodities, container supply, container market values, and disposal costs. The studies employ both simple and advanced statistical methods for analysis. A key finding has been that market liquidity is the primary driver of freight rate fluctuations, which aligns with results obtained using vector autoregression models. Notably, this research has also produced robust predictions of future freight rates with significant improvements achieved through combining indicators through voting mechanisms.

Certain triangulated models of spacetime have been found to exhibit nonsingular "big bang" scenarios that seamlessly transition from a "big crunch". However, these findings are limited to static fabric spaces, where the triangulation doesn't change.

Graph neural networks have grown in popularity for analyzing complex structures, but their intricate designs have made them hard to fully grasp. Although various techniques have been proposed to simplify their operations, they often fail to provide a clear understanding of the complex interactions within the graph structures. This study introduces a novel technique, Acquired Sparsification (AcqSpars), which simplifies GNNs by selectively removing specific node features to make their functions easier to interpret. AcqSpars can be viewed as a targeted form of feature pruning that identifies the most valuable node features for GNN performance. By integrating the feature selection process into the training of the GNN, AcqSpars simultaneously enhances the model's performance and provides a clear picture of the important node features that contribute to the complex interactions within the graph structures. Experimental results on multiple datasets and GNN architectures demonstrate that the features selected by AcqSpars align with human expectations and that the model's performance improves as a result of the structural sparsification. AcqSpars offers a new approach to providing clear functions for GNNs by focusing on the node features that matter most in the graph structures.

A popular dimension reduction technique, introduced by Charikar et al. in 2002, is now being used extensively across multiple disciplines. Our key finding, however, reveals a critical shortcoming of the classic implementation of this technique: it cannot handle the challenge of adaptive adversarial counts effectively. In fact, in the online adversarial settings, even the simplest count-based dimension reduction algorithms experience an unmanageable growth in error, increasing linearly with time. In contrast, in contrast, in the stochastic setting or when faced with oblivious adversaries, CS sketches can achieve dimension reduction performance comparable to their deterministic counterparts. Furthermore, we have developed an improved randomized counting technique that significantly improves upon previous results for counts provided by an adaptive adversary, seeing a dimension growth that only increases by a factor of $\sqrt{T}$ over time.

This research builds upon previous findings and applies findings from that work to the manifold $M$. Given a conformally related metric $\tilde{g}$ within the class $[g]$, we demonstrate that on a sufficiently small domain $\Omega$ within $M$, $\tilde{g}$ can be expressed as a smooth transformation of another metric $g_1$ that possesses the same conformal relationship to $g$. The metric $g_1$ possesses a bounded scalar curvature and its Riemann curvature tensor grows at a rate of $O(d^{-2})$, where $d$ represents the distance from a fixed reference point, provided that this distance is less than $1$. Furthermore, these findings are extended to include higher-order derivatives of the Riemann curvature tensor of $g_1$. Given any desired bound $K$ on the $m$-th order derivatives of the Riemann curvature tensor within a coordinate system, we show that this bound can be achieved on a domain of size $K^{-1/ m}$ with a bound of approximately $1$.

A key feature of superfluids is their ability to form quantized vortices that interact in complex ways. When these vortices are densely packed, they can undergo a phase transition, resulting in a liquid that exhibits unique properties. This liquid exhibits a unique flow resistance, as viscosity arises from scattering events between the vortices. Moreover, the liquid's entropy can be regulated by a chemical potential associated with the interactions between the vortices. As a result, the flow resistance can be modified, and the liquid can exhibit a flow resistance that is directly proportional to its entropy, similar to fluids described by the Mott criterion. Furthermore, an equilibrium between the liquid and its gaseous state can be established, with a boundary that is determined by a balance between the surface tension and the chemical potential associated with the interactions between the vortices.

Advanced prediction and control systems have been developed and refined for complex dynamic environments, yet they often fail to account for how prior knowledge can influence future expectations. To address this concept, we created a flexible framework that integrates prediction and control, enabling real-time adaptation of information from unknown environments and learning of causal connections from non-learning-friendly (non-stationary) settings. This innovation allows for significant improvements in performance when dealing with high-frequency data. Building on this, we designed a new algorithm capable of implementing efficient real-time learning and adaptation within this framework. Our results demonstrate that the problem can be solved with minimal errors that decrease over time, assuming the environment is predictable, and we observed substantial improvements in performance in unpredictable (non-stationary) settings through experiments with multiple vehicles in a driving simulation.

The rise of deep learning has enabled the development of sophisticated models for predicting stock prices. In this research, a hybrid approach combining a language processing model (BERT) and a generative adversarial network (WGAN) is explored to generate highly accurate time series data for a particular stock (NVIDIA). By integrating these cutting-edge technologies, our primary objective is to demonstrate their efficacy in achieving superior results compared to conventional machine learning algorithms. Notably, our innovative framework is designed to be adaptable and can be applied to various industries and markets with minimal adjustments.

This paper introduces a shared envelope formalism called SCATTER, which leverages shared attention mechanisms to facilitate a modular and pre-trained event-level analysis in shared attention structures. Firstly, we enhance the performance of shared attention mechanisms by integrating a class of shared envelopes that unify all attention weights into a single shared envelope that represents the importance of each token across all heads and classes. This formulation not only provides a more comprehensive perspective but also offers interpretability. Moreover, the shared envelope framework is flexible and can be expanded by incorporating pre-trained shared envelopes from other models, allowing for a modularity that is lacking in traditional shared attention mechanisms. Lastly, we focus on a shared attention mechanism that integrates linear shared envelopes and the SCR model, which combines SCR attention weights and a shared envelope that represents the importance of each token. We demonstrate that the SCR model can be interpreted as a linear combination of token-level embeddings and that it outperforms other shared attention mechanisms in a pre-trained event-level analysis of crime reporting.

Our calculations examine the production of two Higgs bosons in a TeV-scale $e^+e^-$ collider within the Standard Effective Field Theory framework at tree level. We determined the production cross section and longitudinal polarisation effects in the process. We also analysed how these findings compare with similar processes within different BSM models including the Standard Model, Two-Higgs Doublet Model, and various quark flavour models. The ability to accurately calculate and measure specific processes at colliders including $\sqrt{s}=3$ TeV will enable a comparison between the number of Standard Model and BSM Higgs in final states that contain highly energetic jets, zero or one $W$ bosons, photons, $T\bar{T}$ and $\gamma\gamma$ among other particles.

We examine the standard approach to deriving a linearized gravity quantum field theory, and show how this approach can be extended to create non-linear general relativity's Einstein gravity theory, as well as a quadratic Lagrangian for the Einstein-Cartan theory. Furthermore, we investigate the gravity Einstein-Cartan theory's relation to gravity's quadratic Einstein-Cartan theory in the presence of non-vanishing torsion.

A new hydrodynamic series expansion has been introduced to solve the hydrodynamic equations of motion numerically, specifically designed to handle localized shocks that propagate laterally in 5D relativistic hydrodynamics. This series expansion takes into account higher-order hydrodynamic effects and is applicable when lateral variations in the shock's amplitude are small. It expands on previous hydrodynamic series by embracing a more complex regime of physics. The series expansion is initiated by a balance between first-order viscous stress and inertial effects, represented as a small perturbation to an exact solution. A general series for the viscosity-to-entropy density ratio $\eta/s$ is derived, with distinct contributions from the viscosity itself, lateral dispersion effects, and entropy generated due to the $1/s$ scaling. The expansion is further utilized to calculate the entropy produced by localized viscous shocks, yielding a series where the leading term is a product of the shock's dissipation in general covariance and entropy flux factors, plus a subleading contribution from lateral dispersion that results in local heating. A series for the stress-energy tensor yields corresponding results for the local energy density and pressure, with the leading term for the energy density being derived from the stress tensor, and the subleading term for the pressure being derived from the stress tensor.

We calculated the drag experienced by a long cylinder moving through a bed of sand, 
either perpendicular or parallel to the flow of the fluid, using a method based on 
force balance. Our model took into account the forces acting on the cylinder from 
both the sand and the fluid. By applying this model to a variety of conditions, 
including different densities and friction levels, we found that our approach 
generally matched experimental data. Notably, we found that the anisotropy of the 
drag experienced by the cylinder was influenced primarily by its aspect ratio, 
rather than the friction level of the sand. Our model also allowed us to 
successfully predict the difference in the drag experienced by the cylinder 
when moving perpendicular and parallel to the flow of the fluid, matching our 
findings with experimental observations.

A major obstacle in comprehending how stars self-regulate on a large scale remains in place. Understanding this phenomenon requires a clear view of outflows from star-forming regions, particularly those triggered by massive stars. Our research overcomes this limitation by utilizing new data from the MUSE survey, which reveals the connection between stars creating outflows and the gas that fuels star formation. Our analysis of 25 high-star-formation-rate galaxies shows that outflows are linked to localized bursts of star formation, with the mass of the newly formed stars directly influencing the outflows. A key pattern emerges when comparing outflows to the "downstream" population of galaxies, where a clear, consistent trend is found. This relationship, known as the wind-track relation, serves as a crucial benchmark for understanding star formation self-regulation. Our modeling of the outflows suggests that a significant portion of gas is expelled from galaxy disks within a short period of time, with similar predictions made for another galaxy sample supporting these findings.

Organizations often generate vast amounts of performance data, which can inform the tuning of complex systems like machine learning models and computer architectures. The goal is to find an optimal configuration that minimizes operational costs. Research into the use of performance models has shown promise in efficiently using data to train models that predict system performance. However, performance models are limited in their ability to accurately model performance across a wide range of data points. OrganizaBo, a novel framework that combines performance models with tree structures and probabilistic reasoning, is proposed to coherently optimize the tuning of highly cost-sensitive systems with numerous parameters. By representing the optimization process as a decision tree and applying probabilistic updates, the purpose of OrganizaBo is to effectively leverage performance models and a large volume of data to optimize system performance while minimizing the cost of operation.

This research analyzes triangular flow using a multiphase transport model for 2013 Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=2.76$ TeV. Cu+Cu collision analysis was performed for transverse momentum ranges $0 < p_T < 4$ GeV/$c$ and $4 < p_T < 8$ GeV/$c$, with $v_n$ coefficients calculated via Fourier transformation. Cu+Cu and Au+Au collisions exhibit similar $v_3$ patterns for $0 < p_T < 4$ GeV/$c$, but differ for $4 < p_T < 8$ GeV/$c$. Measured $v_3$ values exceed expected values from a relativistic hydrodynamic model, particularly in Au+Collisions, whereas $v_3$ data and theoretical predictions align for Cu+Cu Collisions.

The Web 3.0 vision relies on connecting various digital resources through a web of data, with RDF datasets forming a crucial foundation. As these RDF datasets grow in size and number, their quality becomes a pressing issue. To address this challenge, we developed a comprehensive framework called REQA that analyzes the structural integrity of large-scale RDF datasets. By focusing on data relationships, REQA provides a method to evaluate the quality of these datasets, allowing for their reliable combination. The system's components can be easily replaced or improved, facilitating adaptation to specific quality requirements. By leveraging distributed computing, REQA is capable of handling massive datasets, a requirement demonstrated through a comprehensive experiment.

When working with stochastic processes that are subject to discrete observation, a common challenge arises from the bias that is inherent in the maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) as a result of the discretization effect. This bias is particularly pronounced when the monitoring interval is large. A common approach to address this issue is to employ correction factors that are derived from the cumulative distribution function of a Gaussian distribution. However, it has been demonstrated that this approach is only valid in the limit as the monitoring interval approaches zero, leaving a significant gap in understanding the bias of the MLE under more realistic conditions. This study seeks to address this issue by developing an alternative estimation method for a diffusion process that is based on the relationship between a maximum and its corresponding value at a given time. A key advantage of this new estimator is that it is not influenced by the Karatzas' identity, which is a fundamental property of Brownian motion. Both analytical and numerical findings indicate that this non-likelihood-based estimator is capable of providing a lower mean squared error than the MLE, especially when the monitoring interval is not extremely short.

We analyzed a Seyfert 1 galaxy, designated as NGC 4051, to investigate its properties. Through a detailed examination of its optical and near-infrared spectra, we discovered a broad Balmer line complex that exhibited characteristics of shock heating. This line complex, situated at the edge of a large-scale spiral arm, was oriented perpendicular to the spiral arm. The line complex was attributed to a line-driven wind, characterized by a low mass outflow rate and speed. This observation, of a line complex exhibiting shock heating outside the direction of ionization from the active galactic nucleus, represents a unique case and provides support for hydrodynamical and magnetohydrodynamical wind models. The line complex was also associated with a line ratio consistent with a line-driven wind. The line complex was also situated at the intersection of two spiral arms. The line complex was located in a dense gas region, which may have contributed to the line formation.
