During the COVID-19 pandemic, a significant amount of misinformation spread rapidly via social media in China, posing considerable challenges to effective epidemic prevention and control. To tackle this issue, we developed a model to analyze the dissemination of online rumors, incorporating a mechanism to assess the impact of information verification. Through parameter estimation based on real-world data, we revealed that a significant portion of misinformation had been amplified by verified information through user sharing. In an effort to curb the spread of online rumors, we analyzed how adjusting key parameters could influence their transmission. Furthermore, we ranked major social media platforms according to their role in the transmission of misinformation. Based on this ranking, we proposed a strategy to mitigate the spread of online rumors: prioritizing the removal of high-transmission, low-impact information, followed by user-targeted interventions aimed at limiting the spread of highly infectious but low-impact rumors.

We are launching the Fornax3D Initiative to explore the evolution of galaxies in the Fornax Cluster through high-resolution 3D models of a selected sample. These remote spheres, which contain all the stellar generations and remnants within each, can be studied in various stages. However, many essential components remain underrepresented in existing data sets, notably nebular structures around active black holes and white dwarfs. To fill this data gap, we will conduct a comprehensive imaging study of the central regions of 40 elliptical galaxies in the Fornax Cluster, utilizing the Subaru Telescope and the Near-Infrared Camera and Multi-Object Device. This will allow us to pinpoint the locations of intermediate-mass black holes and measure their masses, as well as map the distribution of X-ray binaries and stellar populations. By combining this new data with existing observations, we aim to develop sophisticated simulations that incorporate each stage of a galaxy's life cycle. To do this effectively, we will employ the power of high-performance computing and utilize the Near-Infrared Spectrograph on the same telescope to obtain stellar velocity data, enabling us to create accurate models of the galaxies' spatial distributions and measure their distances. To facilitate the analysis of this extensive data set, we will create a user-friendly web interface known as the Fornax3D Portal, which will also serve as a platform for the publication of our findings and the creation of detailed scientific papers.

Stream processing systems are responsible for handling and analyzing data that is continuously being generated. In recent years, these systems have been employed in a wide range of applications, from monitoring server performance to tracking changes in financial markets. Stream processing engines form the core of these systems, however, existing designs have not fully optimized for efficiency when processing data that is consistently being created. In this paper, we explore various aspects of stream processing, including how to efficiently manage updates to periodic data sets through specialized techniques and hardware components. As a result, we have developed a high-performance stream processing engine called LifeStream, which demonstrates significant improvements in efficiency through both simulation and testing on real hardware.

A time-like Bertrand curve in a Riemannian manifold is defined by the property that its corresponding reverse curve in the same manifold is also a Bertrand curve, and this relationship holds true for these curves.

Deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success in various applications, particularly in fields like speech recognition and classification. However, these models are typically trained using gradient descent to minimize a loss function, which significantly impacts their performance. We investigate the effects of modifying the target variable in a simple classification problem to determine if alternative loss functions can lead to more robust models. We evaluate two distinct training scenarios and find that models trained with a modified loss function exhibit a notable increase in permutationally distinct generalizations by a factor of up to 1000 compared to models trained with the standard cross-entropy loss. This result suggests that models with better generalization capabilities can be achieved with a model architecture that remains unchanged.

A stabilization method for the 2D and 3D Navier-Stokes equations is presented, 
achieved through a boundary feedback control applied to a non-collateral boundary. 
The control law's simplicity is highlighted, with only linear observations and controls involved. 
To examine the feasibility of this approach, H^2 regularity results for the domain are H^1 regularity results for the control are explored.

This research utilizes a newly created numerical model to simulate the complex process of strain-induced crystallization in natural rubber. The model incorporates a fully 3D mechanical model that accounts for the development of crystalline structure within the material, based on an energy-based criterion first proposed by Markovitz in 1965. Using a combination of the ABAQUS/Standard mechanical solver and a user-defined material routine, the model successfully predicts the crystalline structure formation resulting from sudden application of tension. Furthermore, it reveals the characteristic stress overshoot and subsequent increase in Young's modulus observed in experimental data, providing evidence for the predicted microstructure's impact on the material's mechanical behavior. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the potential of fully 3D energy-based criteria in predicting the microstructure development of soft materials and how that structure influences their mechanical properties.

To understand the magnetic properties of triplet Cooper pairs in nematic superconductors, we calculated the equilibrium magnetization resulting from the impact of a weak external magnetic field. Using the Gor'kov formalism, we found that the density of the absorbed spin moment is directly related to the Pauli paramagnetic effect, with the magnitude of this relationship determined by the superconducting gap's anisotropy. The calculated formula for the equilibrium spin density is valid within the weak external field limit, allowing it to describe the density of the hot Fermi surface. This model was then applied to the superconducting state of monolayer MoS2, and our results indicate that the critical limits of the external field vary in response to the Fermi surface density and the BCS coupling constant.

A significant hurdle in learning optimal actions for a robot is accessing feedback that clearly indicates success or failure from a human supervisor. To address this challenge, various reward functions have been developed, including feedback from a human through observation or direct communication. However, mere positive reinforcement is not always enough, as a human may need to intervene and guide the robot by correcting its mistakes, for instance, by physically adjusting the robot during a task. This direct feedback provides not only a signal of success or failure but also explicit information about what went wrong and how to rectify the error. Unfortunately, this feedback is not always readily available and may need to be processed in real-time. To overcome this challenge, a promising solution is to leverage machine learning algorithms that are fueled by mere success or failure feedback, for instance, through the use of a shaping algorithm that breaks the task into smaller, more manageable parts, for instance, by dividing the task into a sequence of sub-tasks. This approach has been widely used in reinforcement learning, for instance, to teach a robot to perform complex tasks, for instance, to grasp and manipulate objects. To further facilitate efficient learning with corrective feedback, a human supervisor may be able to provide local information about the environment and the robot's current state, for instance, by guiding the robot through a series of targeted trials. This direct feedback may be used to accelerate the robot's ability to infer the value of different actions, for instance, by providing a more accurate estimate of the return that can

Difference Differential Continuous Phase Modulation (DCPM) detection without a reference frame has long-standing advantages over frame-based methods in terms of delay and frame length requirements. However, it comes with a drawback of needing a delay equal to two base time intervals. Now, we demonstrate that for any chosen greater delay values, there exists a differential detection method that maintains robustness against impairments such as filtering, amplitude and frequency mismatches, and multiple paths. Notably, this differential method can even work with very short frame differences, potentially even as short as one sample.

We investigate the ability of next-generation gravitational wave and electromagnetic observatories to detect black-hole neutron-star mergers. Using detailed simulations of core-collapse supernovae, we found that some events produce neutron stars while others result in direct black-hole formation. Our study reveals that electromagnetic signals from these supernovae can be weak due to the mass-energy of the newly formed compact object being swallowed by the accretion disk. Consequently, a significant number of cases where matter is ejected do not produce bright electromagnetic sources. Therefore, the ability to detect such mergers using gravitational waves and electromagnetic signals will be significantly reduced.

The nature of dark energy and its potential link to vacuum breakdown in spacetime remains a mystery. To shed light on this issue, we propose using quantum capability and compressibility as indicators of spacetime stability. The compressibility of spacetime can be quantified through the speed of sound, which, in the case of the $\Lambda$CDM model, decreases over time, raising questions about its physical plausibility. Our research indicates that the quantum capability of spacetime in the $\Lambda$CDM model exceeds the speed of light in the early universe, but falls below it in the current and future universe. To overcome these limitations, we present a new dark energy model that ensures the quantum capability of spacetime remains below the speed of light both in the early and late universe. Furthermore, our analysis using supernovae, cosmic microwave background, and baryonic acoustic oscillation data reveals that the compressibility of spacetime in the $\Lambda$CDM model and our new model exhibits distinct characteristics.

The proposed framework addresses the simultaneous generation of rain and cleaning of rain-affected images.  A discrete autoencoder is employed to encode clear images and encode synthetic rain images, with the model trained to achieve mode separation in the latent space.  Once rain elements are created in the clear image's mode, the model's rain decoder generates rain-affected images.  Furthermore, the clear image's mode acts as a target for the latent space of synthetic rain images, allowing the model to create rain-free images from rain-affected images.  Implementing simultaneous rain creation and removal in this manner demands real-time action on both the encode and decode components of the model.  Experimental evaluations demonstrate the proposed method's ability to accurately create rain in clear images and remove rain from rain-affected images.

A group ranking approach is now widely used for learning reward functions in complex tasks, such those evaluated via image data. However, traditional methods require substantial computational resources, requiring every individual option to be separately ranked, which is both costly and inefficient. Our research proposes a novel, resource-friendly method that leverages visual data to quickly determine the relative worth of multiple, simultaneously presented options. By presenting sets of concurrent options, organized into separate groups, and rapidly ranking these groups, our method significantly reduces the number of required data samples required to train effective reward models. We demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of our method by adapting an existing large-scale visual data set for model training, outperforming both existing algorithms and random approaches in our experiments.

A new approach to understanding continuum entanglement transitions within a broad range of models is introduced, based on a specific model class that includes various theories of non-interacting fermions on lattices or fields with parities preserved. A key finding from this class is that the critical magnetic field at which spin entanglement transitions occur is directly influenced by the spatial dimensions of the system, and this relationship can be accurately predicted using the asymptotic formula ΔB/B ~ 1/W, where W is the width of the system. This approach leads to a set of testable predictions regarding the entanglement properties of continuum models, and a detailed examination of the 2D Anderson model reveals a strong correlation between its behavior and that of this proposed model class.
This study investigates how a particular curvature, related to Q, behaves within specific bounded areas of space.

Given the rising number of road accidents caused by drivers who have consumed drugs or alcohol, there's a pressing need to create an effective system for preventing such incidents. This research proposes using a five-factor model of personality to assess a person's likelihood of engaging in risky behavior while under the influence of drugs or alcohol. We used factor analysis to ascribe meaning to the latent variables in the five-factor model and then applied a logistic regression to examine the model's ability to predict drug use risk. The results indicate that this approach can successfully classify individuals into high-risk and low-risk categories based on their personality traits, achieving accuracy rates of 0.85 and 0.7 respectively. However, further research with a larger sample size is necessary to validate these findings.

We introduce a significant innovation in common sense reasoning called Machine Common Knowledge (MCK), an atlas of if-then statements that capture a broad range of everyday, common sense knowledge known to multiple people, machines, or systems. An all-encompassing if-then knowledge base is what constitutes an atlas of machine common sense knowledge (ATOMIC). If-then representations of a large amount of domain-specific knowledge, covering nearly 900,000 facts about 100,000 entities, are then created by our proposed method, a new large-scale method that combines expert annotation, human labeling, and large language model (LLM) inference. If-then statements of complex scientific, historical, and business knowledge are successfully annotated in three case studies that demonstrate human annotation feasibility, high quality, and LLM's complementary capabilities. An experiment that pits LLMs trained on our quality control dataset against human annotators shows that if-then reasoning with LLMs and an MCK atlas yields higher accuracy rates than models without an MCK atlas. An exploration of LLM's complementary capabilities to human annotators shows that they excel in areas of low human agreement, a phenomenon that we hypothesize to be a manifestation of Schelling's focus effect. An all-encompassing if-then statement that captures the entirety of common sense knowledge is then proposed to be the future of machine intelligence.

This paper introduces NISQ-HHL, a new method for solving sparse, positive, diagonal-dominant systems of linear equations, building upon the well-known HHL algorithm.  NISQ-HHL overcomes previous limitations of HHL by eliminating the requirement for unitary diagonalization and reducing the need for phase estimation.  We demonstrate a significant improvement in polynomial factors for query complexities of two critical parameters in quantum linear algebra.  Specifically, NISQ-HHL achieves a much lower QSP depth, ideal for solving practical applications on near-term hardware, while maintaining robustness to operational errors.  In contrast, our variant increases reliance on the inverse of the system's maximum eigenvalue.  A detailed analysis of the NISQ-HHL is provided, highlighting its optimal performance in certain scenarios.  NISQ-HHL may be viewed as an extension of the HHL, potentially useful for portfolio optimization in our study.  We also present a prototype implementation using the IBM quantum computer, which successfully solved an instance of the problem on near-term hardware and simulated systems of up to 20 equations.

Recently, pre-trained language models have significantly boosted performance in various NLP tasks. To further enhance these models, researchers have begun exploring multi-modal training using both speech and text data. In this study, we introduce a novel multi-modal training approach called Bidirectional Focus (BFOCUS). This framework involves training language models with both speech and text data, where each data type helps resolve ambiguities specific to the other modality's vocabulary. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed BFOCUS framework yields substantial improvements over previous methods with comparable dataset sizes. Furthermore, it allows for significant gains using only text data as a pre-training step. Our research results also indicate that the order in which speech and text data are trained does not impact the final outcome.

The n-th average cross section is calculated by summing the coordinate differences multiplied by the average slope between adjacent points on a parametric curve from t-a to t+b. This concept builds on work by Hadwiger and Minkowski, extending their work on average perimeter and width concepts. Our research expands on these ideas by defining average cross section and proving that for a parametric curve enclosing a closed area, the average cross section is related to the average width and perimeter. The connection to average brightness is also explored. The research further demonstrates that for convex curves, having a constant average cross section as a function of curve parameters implies the curve is an ellipse.

For a randomly chosen parking function from S_n, its characteristic degree k defines it. We investigate the distribution of characteristic degrees by analyzing the number of elements with a specific key value in the pair (i, i mod 2) for all 'i' from 1 to 'n'.

Researchers investigated the electrical properties of superconducting NbN nanowires, which were patterned into narrow channels and covered with gate electrodes. As the thickness of the NbN layer decreased, they found that random fluctuations in charge could be controlled by the electrodes, leading to a type of insulating behavior where conductivity changed in discrete steps. This controlled conductivity could switch between two states in response to voltage fluctuations, and was most prominent in very thin superconducting materials. The influence of these volume charges was further confirmed by the observation of negative capacitance. Additionally, the study found that increasing the gate voltage could trigger transitions from an insulating state to a superconducting state, and that this transition was made easier by the accumulation of electrons, particularly in wider nanowires.

Spectra of T-dwarfs exhibit striking similarities to L-dwarfs, yet with reduced features and increased symmetry. To fully grasp the atmospheric composition of T-dwarfs, a comprehensive study is required. GJ 229B, being the most thoroughly studied T-dwarf, exhibits H- and K-band spectra that exhibit unusual features, possibly indicative of thermal inversion. To investigate this, we employed the ExoPlanet Atmospheric Inverse Line Of-Fourier Transform (ExoPlanet Atmospheric) retrieval code to analyze the H- and K-band spectra of GJ 229B, using a grid of 3D atmospheric models. Our results suggest a thermal inversion in the upper atmosphere of GJ 229B, characterized by increased oxide molecule opacity in the visible spectrum. We also explored the impact of non-equilibrium chemistry on the spectra, finding that it has a significant impact on H-band features but not on the observed unusual K-band features. Our equilibrium chemistry assumption suggests a surface gravity of approximately 2.5 m/s^2 and effective temperatures between 600-800 K, which is inconsistent with other studies. Non-equilibrium chemistry allows for a broader range of possible effective temperatures, which is indicative of unresolved gaseous composition, possible vertical temperature gradients, and possible cloud/deep convection impacts.

The nature of the quark-gluon medium is extensively studied through the observation of high-energy particle behavior. By analyzing the final particle distribution, physicists can deduce properties of this medium. However, a more direct method of study involves measuring the particles' mean free path. This study aims to provide a detailed, quantitative assessment of a particle's interaction length as it moves through the quark-gluon medium. Initial findings suggest that a gluon may travel approximately one femtometer before undergoing an inelastic collision, while quarks may have an even shorter interaction length. Quantifying this behavior will enable us to better understand and model the dynamic processes occurring within the quark-gluon medium.

Current methods for predicting road scenes rely heavily on advanced processing of visual data, overlooking the basic pattern repetition observed in many ordinary video clips. This study presents a straightforward and effective approach to predicting road scene images by examining previous images, bypassing the need for sophisticated image feature extraction and learning techniques. In fact, a simple strategy proves most successful in this task - research indicates that 90% of accuracy can be achieved without any learning, while utilizing the remaining 10% of data to learn a basic transformation significantly boosts performance.

Multielectron systems with interactions between electrons in different orbitals and spins are notable for producing phenomena such as inter-orbital symmetry breaking, permanent polarization, inter-orbital entanglement, and inter-orbital magnetism. However, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between these effects and their analogous phenomena is still lacking due to the difficulty in independently controlling different occupied orbitals. Researchers have recently managed to isolate and control three specific potassium atoms occupying the $4s$ and $4p$ orbitals using optical traps, which has led to a breakthrough in detecting inter-orbital exchange interaction through the observation of spin polarization and long-lived entanglement when electrons in $4s$ and $4p$ orbitals are coupled with electrons in $4p$ orbitals. Furthermore, this study has demonstrated that certain types of inter-orbital interactions can be stronger than Coulomb repulsion, which has significant implications for developing more efficient methods for information processing.

The Omega baryon, specifically the $\Omega^{-}$ with unique quark composition of $sss$, has long been the subject of theoretical study. Now, with experimental evidence for it obtained at the BEPCII/BCI using the HBC detector, we present a comprehensive analysis of its various forms. Our calculations, which consider spin-dependent forces, incorporate experimental data to provide accurate predictions for the $\Omega^{-}$ baryon's spectrum, along with relevant decay information. We also explore the impact of compact matter on the quark dynamics, revealing that increased density can lead to significant shifts in the baryon's decay properties.

Regarded as a beneficial modeling technique, the well-mixed framework may misrepresent the rapid transmission of respiratory diseases that occur in confined spaces, such as those on public transportation. This can lead to inaccurate predictions when applying this model to understand the spread of illnesses like COVID-19. This paper will utilize a more precise compartmental transmission model to compare with outcomes derived from the well-mixed model, specifically examining the speed of disease spread in a city bus. By comparing mathematical predictions to observed cases of influenza on public transportation in Israel, we found that the performance of the two models is comparable, yet they provide distinct insights. The analysis revealed that the optimal duration for maintaining social distancing on a bus to effectively reduce the probability of disease spread is around 10 to 15 minutes, a finding supported by a corroborative analysis using stochastic models. The proposed solution is to implement bus routing that minimizes the number of passengers boarding and alighting at the same time across multiple stops, a strategy we also explored using the influenza on a bus case study.

Evaluating quantum vacuum birefringence and light scattering would demand extremely high magnetic fields for the interaction. However, the detection methods proposed are not limited to this specific scenario and can also be applied to any case where particles interact in quantum vacuum under the influence of strong fields. Furthermore, proposed schemes do not directly compare to existing ones, but they offer significantly improved sensitivity through highly efficient photon detectors capable of detecting even single photons, and by utilizing long interaction times and extensive sample areas in the detection process.

This note presents an innovative technique to derive the vertex configuration from the edge configuration in highly symmetric 3D shapes. By applying this approach, the complete structure of the pericosi dodecahedron can be deduced from its edge configuration alone.

We revisit and reexamine the proof of the unforgeability of Public Key Encryption (PKE) schemes under chosen ciphertext attacks, as demonstrated in the pioneering work of Goldwasser, Micali and Shamir (STOC 1985). Our analysis reveals that the original proof contains an oversight, yet we delve into their argument to (1) achieve the desired security through verifiable encryption and (2) circumvent the need for a trapdoor in the PKE scheme, utilizing randomly generated keys instead.

Physical layer authentication relies on device-specific characteristics for identifying legitimate users and distinguishing them from impostors. Traditionally, extracting these unique features requires prior calibration and enrollment at both the transmitter and receiver. A new approach is introduced that omits the need for shared secret keys, enabling the detection of authorized devices in Gaussian noise channels. This method employs a singular value decomposition to achieve this keyless verification. Although initially counterintuitive, it is demonstrated that shared device features can effectively serve to differentiate them from features that vary. Through theoretical analysis and numerical simulations, it is established that incorporating more signal observations enhances performance, with the method approaching an optimal efficiency. Furthermore, it is determined that in noisy conditions, a method utilizing the full decomposition outperforms one relying solely on the first component. This superiority becomes more pronounced with increased noise. Additionally, it is confirmed that this method surpasses a method based on amplitude and phase extraction in terms of accuracy.

We've analyzed the twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides, specifically 2H-$TMDs$, to study their flat-band surface plasmon polaritons. By incorporating twisted degrees of freedom into the $\pm 2e/ħ$ Berry curvature, we found that the surface plasmon polariton flux significantly influences the plasmo-hall effect and can be adjusted through interlayer coupling. This ability to manipulate the plasmo-hall effect may offer new approaches to study this phenomenon. In addition, we observed that plasmons within distinct sectors of momentum space interact due to the plasmo-hall effect, which could be used to create a CO-HAM effect that can be controlled, providing a method to study strong plasmon-correlated phenomena.

This research paper focuses on analyzing the properties of a specific type of geometric structure called a nontrivial gradient Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold. By studying this structure, we have established that a nearly conformal Ricci soliton on a Sasakian manifold must be $\epsilon$-Kahler Ricci flat. We have also derived that the underlying Ricci tensor of this geometric structure is of the type $\eta$-Ricci soliton, where this new classification combines features of both Ricci solitons and gradient Ricci solitons in a Sasakian manifold setting.

This study provides an updated overview of how stellar winds and their variations impact celestial bodies and planetary magnetospheres. We discuss the fundamental principles behind magnetospheres and how they're affected by rotating stars with pulsations and superflares, as well as the behavior of magnetospheres in white dwarfs and neutron stars. We also explore how stellar flares and eruptions can alter planetary magnetospheres, as seen in case studies like Jupiter's Io and Io's magnetosphere. Additionally, we highlight discrepancies between Jupiter's and Jupiter's Io's magnetospheres. We compare Jupiter's and Jupiter's Io's magnetospheres in terms of their magnetic fields and plasma characteristics. We contrast Jupiter's and Jupiter's Io's magnetospheres in terms of their magnetic fields and plasma characteristics. We discuss how Jupiter's magnetosphere is affected by its tilt and how Jupiter's magnetosphere is impacted by its thick atmosphere. Spin-orbit proximity effect is a significant phenomenon to study in heavy metal/ferromagnetic metal pairs due to its potential application in increasing the spin-orbit torque experienced by the ferromagnetic layer. Although the origin of the spin-orbit proximity effect has been observed in various combinations of heavy metal and ferromagnetic metal, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear in Co-based multilayers exhibiting large spin-orbit torques. This study focuses on spin Hall and proximity-induced contributions in a Bi/Co multilayer system, examining the impact of increased total spin-misalignment thickness on both components of the spin Hall and spin-orbit proximity currents. Employing first-principles calculations, variations in the spin currents are modeled as a function of the Bi/Co total thickness, considering both spin Hall and spin-orbit proximity currents. The theoretical model's predictions are verified through measurements of the spin Hall and spin-orbit resonance frequencies in a Bi/Co strip using microwave ferromagnetic resonance.

This paper utilizes the Jumarie type fractional derivative to analyze the time-independent fractional Schrödinger equation associated with a generalized Mie-like potential in multiple dimensions. By applying the semi-it transformation method, we obtain approximate solutions to the modified time-dependent fractional Schrödinger equation. Additionally, we illustrate our approach by solving a fractional Schrödinger equation linked with the generalized Mie-like potential in higher dimension.

We propose a novel perspective on training neural networks by viewing them as approximations of consistent Lipschitz functions. This perspective enables us to introduce a new optimization criterion, specifically the penalty for exceeding a maximum allowed rate of change, to enforce this consistency. By integrating this criterion into the standard loss function used in supervised learning, we establish a unified framework for various regularization techniques, including weight decay, spectral regularization, and sparsity-inducing penalties. This framework is particularly useful in cases where we lack prior knowledge about the appropriate level of penalty. We develop efficient methods to train neural networks by leveraging convex optimization techniques and prove that our proposed regularization ensures uniform convergence rates for the best possible consistent model as the network size decreases.

Sequential neural networks like LSTMs excel at handling lengthy dependencies in language. To explore their effectiveness in capturing morphological agreement in Basque, a highly agglutinative language, we assembled a specialized dataset and conducted an experiment. By examining the results, we found that Basque LSTMs can indeed capture agreement patterns across multiple word boundaries within a single sentence, but this capability is not entirely seamless.

Astronomers used multiple telescopes to observe the HD 80606 b planet as it passes in front of its star. These observations were complemented by data from astrometry and radial velocity to create a detailed timeline for the planet's movement in its orbit. A new method combining these techniques resulted in exceptionally precise predictions of the planet's future movements, with even minor discrepancies already apparent. Using specific measurement standards, our model provides excellent fits for all observations, giving us confidence that this method can accurately predict similar events for other exotic planets. As a result, we can now confidently schedule observations for upcoming missions like James Webb Space Telescope.

Virtual reality gaming is an effective tool for stroke recovery that motivates patients and facilitates relearning of motor skills. A key aspect of these therapies is the reward system, which research indicates strongly correlates with successful rehabilitation. This study explores the application of machine learning to develop accurate student-t $\left(2^{nd}$ order Markov chain\right)$ models of gameplay, which are then used to create tailored, statistically-based custom controls for users. We compared the efficacy of these tailored controls in enhancing perceived game experience and enjoyment, as well as frequency of game engagement, when existing models were found to impede progress. We also examined the potential of these techniques to enhance rehabilitation by simulating stroke effects and developing strategies to mitigate their impact on a user's performance. We achieved this through a combination of machine learning models and tailored controls, which we tested on 24 healthy participants and 24 participants who had experienced a stroke. Our results showed that participants with a stroke required more trials to reach proficiency but still gained comparable improvements in perceived game experience and enjoyment, as well as frequency of game engagement, when existing models were found to impede their progress and were helped by a combination of statistical cues and tailored controls.

This paper offers a novel variational approach to model broken structures, which accounts for potential discontinuities and large deformations within separate fragments. The proposed framework generates a sequence of more granular models that ultimately describe a system of disconnected components. This study proves that the final model can be represented by a singular functional, whereas earlier variations were capable of describing deformations in single, continuous entities. Furthermore, the paper investigates the conditions under which two separate entities can be merged into one, based on a novel, two-part variational definition.

We examine the Drell-Yan production of a scalar leptoquark $Q_1$ in quark-antiquark annihilation and pair creation in hadron collisions, considering both processes as they have comparable contributions to final state lepton pairs at the LHC with the CMS detector. Current bounds on leptoquark mass from single top production and Drell-Yan of charged lepton pairs suggest similar limits for $\lambda_{Q_1} \sim 1$. To address this, we detail a setup for precise predictions of such processes, incorporating the Catnip framework for next-to-leading order QCD calculations with simulated parton showers. Using proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV, we find cross-section results for Drell-Yan of $Q_1$ that vary significantly with its mass, allowing us to estimate a $\lambda_{Q_1}$ dependent limit of $1.1-1.5$ TeV.

Radiology patients are being increasingly exposed to ionizing radiation as PET scans continue to gain popularity. Advances in PET technology have enabled faster and higher-resolution imaging, but the higher spatial-temporal accuracy comes at the cost of increased exposure to radiation. Deep learning-based methods have shown potential for reducing radiation exposure by processing low-quality PET images and generating high-quality results, but they often struggle with clinically relevant cases outside of their training data due to their reliance on statistical models. To address this limitation, we propose a reduced-dose PET framework that utilizes uncertainty-aware multimodal deep learning in combination with robust physics-based image processing and relies on MRI guidance to overcome the challenges posed by low-quality PET images. This uncertainty-aware framework enables accurate estimation of data-driven uncertainties in PET images, which can be integrated with statistical covariances to produce more reliable results. Our experiments on synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that this new model outperforms existing deep learning approaches in handling reduced-dose PET scans, even in data outside of their training set, and achieves comparable or better performance to state-of-the-art methods on standard datasets.

This study proposes a framework to integrate personalization and data security into the Internet of Things (IoT) environment. We outline a set of requirements and present a prototype system that incorporates a privacy-aware, customizable language for smart devices. Our framework allows IoT entities to exchange a privacy and personalization policy known as CPP, which is negotiated through this language. We demonstrate the feasibility of our approach by creating a smart home scenario and a proof-of-concept application.

A recent shift in the context of coreference resolution is the subject of this paper.
We examine the potential of centering theory to enhance the current context-based resolution methods.
To validate our approach, we introduce a context modeling framework that leverages pre-trained language models, specifically BERT, to better capture contextual centering variables.
Our results indicate that integrating these centering theory concepts can lead to more effective context representation and a significant reduction in computational costs.
Moreover, we can achieve a notable improvement in performance by employing minimal context cues, such as the most recent sentence, to predict theoretical centering elements.
Our proposed method has been tested on two prominent English coreference resolution datasets, with a focus on determining the optimal context length.
Unexpectedly, we found that using just one previous sentence to predict centering theory's left edge feature can result in a substantial reduction in parameters and computational costs, while maintaining a comparable level of performance.

Upward plane drawings of rooted ordered trees are those where the vertices of the tree are positioned in accordance with their parent-child relationships, specifically, a parent is always placed higher than its children. This concept has been expanded for general graphs by considering a partial embedding of a graph into a directed grid, where the y-coordinate of every vertex is less than or equal to that of its parent, thus making the edges point upwards. Researchers have sought to determine the minimum amount by which we need to scale these graphs' coordinates in order to achieve upward planarity. This parameter, known as the upward planar width of a tree, can be calculated efficiently for trees in a polynomial amount of time.

In computer system research, creating a reliable setup that replicates real-world conditions is a crucial and time-consuming task. This paper outlines a framework called RAS that automates the entire setup process using an explicit configuration language specifically designed for this purpose. RAS allows for defining complex system configurations, such as multiple computer setups, easily, which can significantly speed up the prototyping process and allow research prototypes to be transferred to real systems with minimal effort. Additionally, the development of RAS has been facilitated by utilizing existing system setup tools, achieving a balance between functionality and ease of use.

In the large N limit of U(N) vector operators, an operator expansion is considered. The central question is whether the subleading terms in this expansion develop a higher degree of separation between subsystems than the leading term. By applying saturation arguments, we demonstrate that in conformal field theories, the subleading terms indeed exhibit enhanced entanglement, assuming the two subsystems have comparable sizes. Additionally, we demonstrate that this result holds for free bosonic models through an explicit calculation.

Recently, WiFi sensing technology has gained significant interest due to its high sensitivity and ability to perform non-line-of-sight measurements. This capability enables the estimation of distance between a source and a receiver, which can be used for location determination. However, traditional methods of location determination based on signal strength and time have notable drawbacks, such as high error rates and low accuracy. In contrast, the one-dimensional range map obtained from WiFi sensing provides a much higher accuracy. This work aims to present techniques for converting the raw data from WiFi sensing into a one-dimensional range map, thereby facilitating direct and accurate range determination without relying on sensing model inversion.

We employ an effective field theory approach to examine the stability of a Dyson Shell, a structure of rotating test particles orbiting a black hole in general relativity. Previous studies have indicated that Lyapunov exponents can be utilized to assess the effectiveness of Dyson Shell information encryption. However, these analyses face a significant issue: negative imaginary components of certain modes' frequencies, which could compromise the Dyson Shell's overall stability. Our investigation aims to address this problem by identifying the precise conditions under which the Dyson Shell can exist stably. Ultimately, our research provides a set of constraints on the total mass of test particles, their average speed, and their angular momentum, which, if met, will guarantee the dyson shell's long-term stability and, as a consequence, the desired lyapunov coefficients values.

In the context of cloud computing, a critical issue arises from the difficulty in accurately identifying failures that occur when services do not meet agreed-upon standards. Although various methods exist to address this problem, they all have a common drawback of relying too heavily on system administrators. To overcome this limitation, an alternative approach is proposed that utilizes peer-to-peer technology to automatically detect and flag SLA breaches in a decentralized manner. This method, which is based on blockchain technology, allows for the identification of SLA breaches in a transparent and accountable manner, free from any single point of control.

Our research investigates how changing the electron beam configuration influences its disruption instability in an energy recovery linear accelerator. We examined various beam configurations including flat and round distributions and assessed their impact on instability in an ERLinac. We developed a 3D particle-in-cell code to analyze beam disruption instabilities in ERLinac and found that different beam configurations produce varying levels of disruption. There exists an optimal configuration that minimes disruption, and for configurations that are more prone to instability, the beam will self-organize into two counter-rotating bundles. Furthermore, our results indicate that even configurations that are initially symmetric can become disruptive due to the non-symmetric nature of the ERLinac cavity.

Scarcity of neutron sources necessitates the development of highly efficient detectors, which should be compact, robust, and capable of withstanding high fluxes. This research presents an outstanding design for a neutron detector, comprising three-dimensional scintillator chips fabricated from p-type silicon, featuring a comprehensive cross-section of neutron-capturing materials such as hydrogen-rich compounds. By employing radiative charge collection in 3D scintillators, this detector minimizes the impact of carrier recombination, which is prevalent in thick detectors. Simulation and experimental data demonstrate the 3D detector's ability to achieve near-complete charge collection, resulting in superior performance metrics, including 99.9% efficiency at a 1cm thickness and 90% uniformity of charge collection. Its remarkable resistance to saturation allows it to endure high fluxes of up to 10^7 n/cm^2/s, which is 100 times greater than conventional planar detectors of comparable dimensions.

Laboratory experiments investigated the adhesion properties of sub-micron dust particles as temperatures rose, simulating the conditions found in protoplanetary discs. It was found that for particles larger than 0.15 microns in diameter, the adhesion force increased significantly as temperatures rose from 300K to 400K due to particles becoming less volatile. For smaller particles, the adhesion force actually decreased over the same temperature range, likely caused by the particles' tendency to melt and stick less effectively. This research highlights the crucial role that temperature plays in determining sticking characteristics and the early stages of planetary formation in a dynamic environment.

Supervised dimension reduction is a statistical issue aimed at preserving essential information from training data to efficiently predict target variables. Dimension reduction techniques are commonly employed for prediction and are also beneficial in visualizing and interpreting data. Despite the prevalence of research on this topic, a significant amount of work remains underexplored. In contrast, dimensionality reduction methods that prioritize prediction are thoroughly investigated. This project focuses on assessing a particular approach, namely Local Fisher Discriminant Analysis. To evaluate its performance, various datasets are analyzed and visualized to assess its predictive and interpretative capabilities. An R package is created to facilitate this evaluation and provide a platform for extending the method.

Multi-robot learning of complex maneuvers under various constraints is an unexplored area that can be addressed using modern neural networks under diverse conditions. Building on existing research, a new framework called Obstacle Avoidance and Complex Motion Neural network (EKMP) is proposed to allow multiple robots to mimic large-scale, constraint-heavy movements from static and dynamic obstacles using a single data set. The OLC-NEural network (EKMP) is an extension of previous OMP models, which is now capable of navigating nonlinear rigid constraints and static obstacles with a single neural network, thus requiring only one data set to train. Furthermore, OLC-NEural network (EKMP) can mimic intricate maneuvers from both static and dynamic obstacles through a combination of model transformations and data adjustments. With these capabilities, OLC-NEural network (EKMP) is an effective solution to the challenge of multi-robot learning of complex maneuvers under various conditions.

We have calculated the one-loop central-emission vertex for massless external particles in four dimensions, which is relevant to $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. This calculation has been performed in a gauge-invariant form and can be expressed in terms of scalar box coefficients that are commonly found in numerical evaluations using the method of regions. Our results are in line with previously obtained checks for non-abelian gauge theories at four loops, and we have derived a four-loop beta function coefficient for non-abelian gauge theories. This derivation is made possible by combining the equality of anomalous dimensions and central charges in such theories, and it yields the value of $-40000$ or $-40000/2$ for an even number of supersymmetries greater than four, which is a key factor in establishing the existence of a CFT in such a scenario.

A novel type of superfluid, belonging to the topological BDI class, can be found in a two-dimensional Rashba Hubbard model with an attractive interaction, based on a square lattice. Using a mean-field approach, researchers identified this superfluid phase and confirmed its existence through both Gaussian and non-Gaussian analyses of low-energy excitations. A set of topological invariants was utilized to design an efficient algorithm, allowing for a detailed exploration of the model's topological characteristics within a complete parameter space, utilizing the exact solution provided by the quantum Monte Carlo method. A set of Rashba spin-orbit coupling and an external magnetic field can lead to the spin-singlet superfluid to become isolated as a distinct, topologically nontrivial region. A set of premeditated SO coupling and magnetic field values can facilitate the creation of Majorana zero modes at defect sites within the system. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we investigated how impurities behave in $YBa_2Cu_3O_{6.95}$ as we varied the type of vortex created by an applied magnetic field. We found that at a critical angle of 45 degrees, there is a marked shift in the movement and alignment of vortices, where any preferred direction in their movement gives way to chaos. This holds true for various kinds of point-like impurities and remains consistent across different levels of doping and temperatures. Our analysis indicates that this phenomenon is caused by lattice symmetry and the way impurities interact with each other, and we propose that this has significant implications for the behavior of cuprate materials.

We've developed a new model for molten polymers, specifically in stretched areas, which are referred to as "brushes." These structures are often found in nature, for example in adhesion structures of certain insects. Unlike typical models, we've created a brush model that can accommodate surfaces which are heavily stretched and molten, and can even be found in complex, curved natural surfaces. This model provides a way to mathematically describe these structures, even in curved surfaces, by formulating a potential energy function that accounts for the density of the brush and the underlying surface. Through the use of the calculus of variations, we can derive the conditions for the lowest energy state of the brush, which can be found in strongly stretched, molten polymer brushes of complex, curved natural surfaces. This approach can be applied to understand the adhesion structures of certain insects, such as the scarab beetle and the rhinoceros beetle, and even in the case of a rhinoceros beetle, our model predicts a molten end exclusion area that has not been observed before and may be testable experimentally. This research also highlights the importance of polymer density in determining the lowest energy state of the brush, and that the traditional model of polymer density may not be accurate in highly stretched brush areas. Overall, our work provides a more comprehensive model for molten polymer brushes, and has significant implications for the design of bio-inspired and nano-scale devices.

Given a graph, a well-known concept is the metric dimension which involves resolving vertices by a minimal subset of vertices. Now we define and investigate the shortened metric dimension - another parameter for graphs - which can also apply to other algebraic structures like Cayley maps and digraphs. We prove that for any graph without a loop, the shortened metric dimension is at most two less than its standard metric dimension. Additionally, we identify specific conditions under which the shortened metric dimension equals one or its maximum possible value relative to its order.

We've developed a full-sky map utilizing 11 years of Fermi-LAT data, taking into account 100 TeV gamma-ray bursts to enhance source variability. By color-coding sources according to their flux fluctuations, we created a unique representation that could be compared to standard sky charts. We also examined the characteristics of variable sources, noting their prevalence in certain energy ranges and their tendency to be found away from the galactic center. We made our scripts and images available for public use on GitHub, inviting collaboration to refine our approach.

A new mechanism is proposed that outperforms the serial dictatorship in social choice theory. Unlike previous improvements, this proposed method allows for infinite agents while retaining basic principles. It is also confirmed through simulation to be highly efficient when limited to a countable number of agents.

We developed an algorithm to identify binary asteroids in past Pan-STARRS1 images, which leverages the system's high frequency of imaging and extensive historical dataset. Our method is based on detecting pairs of asteroids that remain consistently observed in the same frame despite varying observation times. We refined this approach by incorporating a color similarity criterion and comparing our results with previously identified binaries. Utilizing this method, we identified 11 potential binary asteroids, which we will analyze in more detail.

This study introduces novel inference methods for evaluating a nonlinear, nonseparable regression model in the context of network data. It specifically addresses the assessment of a partially linear model through simulation and real-world application, using an example to analyze peer influence within social networks. To begin, the research formulates an identification strategy for the fully nonparametric model, then proceeds to inferential methods for both the general and partially linear cases. However, due to the difficulty in directly estimating standard errors in highly nonlinear models, it suggests a semi-parametric quasi-experimental approach. Inference is based on the large-sample approximation of the score process and relies on the rate of convergence for the estimated score. Ultimately, it provides results from simulations and an analysis of a dataset that examines peer influence.

This study introduces novel expressions for the variable-order Riemann-Liouville integral and differential operators applied to the sum of two differentiable functions, filling a gap in existing research. Several proofs for this novel formulation are provided. Furthermore, specific instances demonstrating the proof's validity are examined using a recent method for assessing the accuracy of numerical solutions to differential equations involving the variable-order Riemann-Liouville differential operator.

Variable gains and time-varying disturbances are common issues in the application of adaptive beamforming for enhancing communication signals in cognitive radio networks. To address this, a new approach based on recursive least squares is developed and analyzed. The new approach is shown through rigorous mathematical proofs to be stable under specific conditions where the variation levels of gains and disturbances are limited. These proofs are based on current variable information, allowing the stability limits of the proposed method to be reached. Through numerical simulations, the effectiveness of the method in balancing noise and interference suppression is demonstrated.

The development of planetary science relies heavily on analyzing spectra from various sources, including spectrographs, imaging spectrometers, and conventional cameras. To facilitate this research, researchers require software capable of processing and visualizing spectra, from simple to complex representations. Additionally, to accelerate data interpretation, these visualization tools should be capable of generating graphics that reflect both spectral and spatial aspects of samples. To facilitate this, we have created a suite of four Python programs – IAS, Spitzer, COAL, and RCSEDv2 – that visualize spectra and full-color images, with all tools accessible via web interfaces powered by Jupyter notebooks and Shiny. To make visualizations user-friendly, we have incorporated the rcse package, an open-source library designed to plot spectra and generate visualizations from a single input file format.

Researchers examined recent seismic events in Southern Brazil, Southern Paraguay, and Northern Argentina to explore a possible link to an intracratonic rift zone extending from the Atlantic Ocean into South America's interior. The analysis focused on the spatial and temporal patterns of these earthquakes, as well as their energy release and associated geological features. Notably, researchers discovered linear concentrations of seismic activity in the interior of South America that align with the Southern Atlantic fissure, particularly in Paraguay and Argentina. This region is characterized by ancient mineralization and geological formations, including the Rio Doce do Sul iron ore and the Parana-Etendeka basalts, which erupted approximately 130 million years ago. These discoveries support the hypothesis of an intracratonic rift zone, potentially related to the opening of the Southern Atlantic Ocean.

The primary challenge in medical image segmentation lies in accurately capturing the boundary information. Due to the inherent data scarcity in medical images, fully supervised approaches are frequently hindered. Thus, partially supervised methods that omit label information have gained considerable attention. However, due to excessive background information, they often suffer from information overload. To tackle these issues effectively, a novel two-pronged strategy is proposed under the fully supervised framework. Initially, an extensive information optimization technique is incorporated to balance informative content extraction and noise reduction. Secondly, a boundary-sensitive mechanism is proposed to emphasize boundary information and suppress unimportant background information. To broaden the applicability, an enhanced information optimization technique is optionally introduced. Comprehensive experiments conducted on public datasets such as RSAT, Synapse, and ACDC demonstrate the superiority of the proposed method over current state-of-the-art algorithms. Furthermore, results from experiments on real-world clinical data verify its effectiveness. All results are fully supervised.

We present a original approach to leading a tabletop role-playing game through a learning-based method. Our proposal, Intents and Theory-of-Mind (ITOM), enables the dungeon master's hand-crafted interactions with players to be supplemented by other agents' learning. Both the environment and the theory-of-mind components learn in response to the dungeon master's guidance, with the former working to model how the dungeon master operates and the latter to predict the outcomes of various decisions. By effectively combining these two, the theory-of-mind agent can make more informed choices. To demonstrate the potential of this approach, we conducted a series of experiments where both the dungeon master and various agents played a crucial role. The results showed that introducing a dungeon master to the ITOM environment led to significant improvements in utility, with both deterministic and stochastic variants outperforming a baseline across multiple trials.

Current Lexical Semantic Change Detection (SCC) approaches primarily rely on human knowledge databases like WordNet, which are not practical for large-scale monitoring. This limitation is exacerbated by the necessity of human involvement in collecting and annotating data. This paper presents an innovative, fully automated method for detecting (temporal) lexical semantic shifts, which surpasses existing approaches in both precision and recall. Our model can pinpoint specific words that have undergone significant semantic changes, outperforming the SODA approach by a notable margin.

We propose a novel set of functions that depend on $k_\perp$ for the polarisation of particles, which are derived from the particles' spin vector and momentum direction. These functions describe the probability density of finding a specific quasiparton, characterized by its longitudinal momentum $x$ and transverse momentum distribution $k_\perp$.

The three-dimensional structure of a protein is intricately determined by the folding patterns that occur in two dimensions within its sequence. Many proteins contain knots, which can be knotted in various ways. Understanding the complex relationship between a knotted protein's three-dimensional structure and the patterns that emerge during folding has long puzzled researchers. New techniques for creating artificial knotted proteins in the laboratory have made it possible to investigate the connection between structure and folding patterns, particularly in relation to how these proteins transition from their linear state to their final, complex shape. This study utilizes advanced topological methods to analyze the three-dimensional structure of knotted proteins in their natural state and identifies a set of virtual loops within the protein's knot. These loops provide insight into the path of bending that occurs as the protein folds, revealing that certain sequences in the protein's linear state correspond to specific three-dimensional shapes that influence how the protein folds into its final, complex shape.

To address the mystery of the universe's matter content, several theories have been proposed, but none have been confirmed. As an alternative, we explore the early dark energy hypothesis, which suggests a universe's matter content includes energy that is neither diluted by expansion nor caused by gravitational interaction. By combining Planck and BOSS data, we analyze the early dark energy hypothesis and calculate its potential limits. By integrating Planck's Planck spectrum and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations from BOSS's DR10 survey, we find the most restrictive constraints on the early dark energy's density today, suggesting that if it exists, its density will have an upper limit of approximately 4.5% of the critical density of the universe. By analyzing the likelihood of different models, we also find that the early dark energy model fits the Planck and BOSS data as well as the $\Lambda$CDM model.

We define two new symplectic groups, connected and disconnected, comprising homotopic mapping classes from the symplectic homotopy category of blown-up tori. The disconnected group SMT(Χ) is demonstrated to be the free product of linear symplectic groups of the blooned tori Χ's components. The disconnected group includes a rich subgroup of the integral symplectic groups as a subgroup of finite index. The connected group, MMT(Χ), is D(Σ(Χ)) mod its first homology group.

A detailed examination of the Nambu-Goldstone (NG) boson theorem's various forms in both relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories has been conducted. An analysis of NG bosons' multiplicity and mass across different theories has been undertaken, with specific emphasis placed on assessing the usual criteria for massless NG boson generation in both frameworks. An exploration of several nontrivial theories has been undertaken, with an analysis of whether or not they result in massless NG bosons, massive NG bosons, or neither, has been conducted. An overview of recent advances involving massive NG modes has been provided.

Current small language generation models effectively replicate target texts but are
unclear in explaining what changes in input lead to variations in output, a crucial
aspect of counterfactual analysis that's often ignored. To address this limitation,
we introduce a new method for extracting explanatory, phrasal counterfactuals from
target outputs utilizing large language generation models. This innovative approach
identifies minimal input alterations that would result in a different output, staying
aligned with the original text's semantic content. Our DISCO method leverages a
gradient-based search to minimize the distance between the original and replicated
counterfactual input representations. We validate this approach on multiple benchmark
datasets, finding it can successfully generate coherent and semantically meaningful
phrasal counterfactual explanations for various NLP tasks including machine
translation, text summarization, and machine naming.

Total coloring of a graph G involves assigning colors to both edges and vertices so that no adjacent or identical elements share the same color. For sum distinguishing total colorings, the color sums of adjacent vertices need to be different. We have developed a general method for creating a closed formula for the chromatic index χsdt(G) of specific types of circulant graphs, and this method is applied to double paths, complete bipartite graphs, and others. Our newly created bound for χsdt(G) can also be derived from existing literature.

Researchers explored how manganites and Heusler materials grow on graphene that sits on top of an aluminum oxide substrate using remote epitaxy. They found a way to control the orientation of these films by adjusting their thickness. For thinner films, they adopt a specific one-dimensional pattern, but for thicker versions, they switch to a different threefold symmetry. To understand this switch, they used calculations based on physics principles and the key is likely related to forces acting between the manganites/Heusler materials and the aluminum oxide. They also used computer simulations to figure out that the relationship between these materials results in very small areas of direct contact. However, even these small areas of contact have a significant impact on the materials' magnetic properties. As a final note, they observed that controlling this interaction may also have applications in using remote epitaxy for other types of materials.

In this paper, we examine $\mathbb{Z}_p \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes, which are defined as $p$-tuples of rows from code matrices with the second code matrix having row indices from the first code matrix. We prove that such a code's dimension equals the sum of the individual code matrices' dimensions, and that the null space of such a code corresponds to the tuple of the individual code matrices' null spaces.

The effectiveness of well intervention techniques relies heavily on the properties of polymer plugs, which are designed to control the flow of fluids in a variety of scenarios. These designs are typically based on numerical modeling, which, however, often fails to account for a key factor: the injection rate at which the polymer is introduced. To address this limitation, a series of high-precision experiments were conducted to observe the behavior of a dilute polymer solution as it is introduced into the same setup used for well modeling. The experiments, in which the injection rate was controlled, revealed the presence of an interface between the polymer and water, as well as a distinct air pocket that forms as the polymer comes to rest. To further analyze the situation, the governing equations were solved numerically, with the resulting model taking into account the friction between polymer chains. When the control of the injection rate was incorporated into the model, it accurately predicted the formation of the interface and air pocket seen in the experiments.

A significant portion of real-world data is labeled in a single-label format, making it challenging to train models for multi-label learning. This paper proposes a novel framework that utilizes data augmentation to generate multi-label samples from single positively labeled data. The proposed method is highly versatile and can be applied to various modalities, including images, texts, and even a combination of both. Our approach is straightforward to implement and requires only an unlabeled data stream. We utilized this framework to enhance a BERT-based multi-label classifier using only a single-label label, achieving top-tier performance on the Amazon reviews dataset without any significant improvements from the increased data volume. Additionally, we used this method to pre-train a BERT-based multi-label sentence pair classifier from single-label Sentiment data, resulting in performance on par with the BERT baseline using the original dataset.

This research provides a rigorous proof that the energy in a specific range never increases over time for both noninteger and integer values of a particular parameter in two time-fractional models. Additionally, the study offers a detailed explanation of how the slow diffusion phenomenon arises from a classical model, specifically involving a rapidly decreasing function.

The Gibbs ensemble represents a fundamental concept in statistical mechanics, where a system's observable properties are derived from those of an underlying system, whose state is a result of an observable entity's status. This relationship can be modeled using a mathematical structure called a double category, where arrows represent systems and cells represent relationships between them. It has been previously shown that a specific type of systems cell, resulting from a combination of relationships, induces a mathematical operation that averages out properties to obtain observable characteristics. Now, a new discovery reveals that the underlying system is actually a result of a mathematical transformation called an adjoint functor, which arises from this systems cell. This adjoint functor establishes a connection between a category of observable properties and a category of system states, effectively providing a mathematical framework for understanding how system states give rise to observable characteristics through a weighted relationship known as a density matrix.

We propose a novel theory to explain the uncharted high-energy gamma-rays from nearby galaxies. This phenomenon cannot be accounted for by conventional models. Instead, we suggest that magnetic fields within captured accretion disks around the central supermassive black holes in these galaxies are responsible. This "captured disk" model effectively describes both the high-energy gamma-rays and the extensive radio emissions from these galaxies through a single, comprehensive mechanism. Additionally, it offers a more realistic representation of magnetic fields within the vicinity of a supermassive black hole compared to standard models. Furthermore, it addresses the long-standing gamma-ray emission mystery in galaxies that lack a central active supermassive black hole.

This study develops advanced portfolio allocation strategies to optimize a portfolio's performance metrics, including value at risk, expected returns, and portfolio variance. We leverage a less-explored aspect of historical price data by treating return values as a three-dimensional series and utilizing slicing techniques to create novel portfolio implementations. Specifically, we employ these methods to develop efficient strategies for both backtesting and real-time execution. Our research demonstrates that this approach yields highly competitive results when compared to industry standards.

Early detection of heart conditions relies heavily on auscultation, the listening to heart sounds. This process, though simple and non-invasive, is prone to background noise interference which can hinder accurate diagnosis. This project's goal was to develop a method for early classification of normal and abnormal heart conditions from phonocardiogram audio that includes added noise. A deep learning-based approach using a ResNet34 architecture achieved a 99% accuracy in distinguishing between normal and abnormal conditions. Furthermore, a custom data augmentation technique was employed to mitigate the effects of noise, resulting in a 99.8% accuracy.

The primary use of mobile and wearable technology has been in medical care, with fitness trackers serving as the most popular examples. These devices can monitor vital signs and provide health insights to users. As a result, researchers are now exploring the potential for federated learning to be applied in the field of medical care using wearable technology. Federated transfer learning can be utilized to allow users to train accurate models with a smaller amount of data by combining data from multiple sources and learning from a larger dataset without sharing sensitive information. In order to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we have tested it on publicly available datasets and found that it can achieve high levels of accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we have developed a framework for federated transfer learning called FedHealth that incorporates secure communication and efficient model training into its design.

This project's essence lies in refining the traditional high-moments portfolio optimization approach by leveraging advanced mathematical transformations and computational algorithms, specifically the change of variables and parallel computing techniques. The objective of portfolio optimization is to identify the ideal balance between risk and return, a challenge that can be addressed by calculating the first few higher-moments of the stock return distribution and formulating an equivalent linear problem. While this method is well-established, our work seeks to enhance its efficiency by streamlining the calculation of these higher-moments and solving the resulting linear equation. To accomplish this, we leverage a hybrid algorithm that combines simulated annealing with linear regression to reduce the number of required evaluations and improve the stability of the solution. The results of our approach are showcased through the application of our method to the AEX index, a Dutch stock index, and demonstrate significant improvements in runtime and solution accuracy when compared to the traditional method. Our findings suggest that by using a more efficient approach to elevated moments portfolio optimization, we can achieve a level of performance that is comparable to the original method, but with a level of consistency that is lacking in the traditional approach.

We propose a new approach to the coincidence dilemma using a12-dimensional space, where the physical space is represented as a special 3-dimensional slice. This approach is more intuitive and visually accessible than previous 11-dimensional methods, such as the original Large Hadron Collider. We illustrate this method using a special class of objects called Azumaya algebras, demonstrating how they can resolve the coincidence dilemma. If necessary, we can substitute Azumaya algebras for other analogous mathematical structures.

This paper presents a new algorithm whose output can be directly used,
streamlining the identification of relevant data in vast online collections.
We designed this algorithm to efficiently process large datasets from public
sources, accelerating their review by bypassing obvious inaccuracies and
technical issues. Unfortunately, existing methods for tackling these issues
and filtering out irrelevant data are largely manual and slow. Our innovative
approach combines relevant background information with a carefully crafted
model that determines the significance of each data entry, enabling their
trillions to be processed within a reasonable timeframe. As a proof of concept,
we applied this method to a major public database of astronomical distances,
and our results show that it can significantly accelerate the discovery of
anomalous data, including previously unidentified potential fraud. Moreover,
we discovered that our model accurately predicts reliable data, and we were
able to demonstrate that it effectively accelerates human reviewers by nearly
four times in relevant experiments.

We tackle a control problem where the cost function undergoes sudden changes in response to the controlled system. Our key innovation is allowing the system to switch between two states with no toggle cost, effectively bypassing the usual difficulty of optimal switching. This approach enables us to prove that the best strategy involves observing and responding to the system's behavior. Given the inherent complexity of the value function, we propose an alternative characterization using a pair of functions that better capture its properties. Furthermore, this characterization helps us establish that the optimal strategy can be determined by observing the system's behavior.

An even-numbered color in leptoquark pairs can lead to uneven distribution of up-type leptoquarks and down-type leptoquarks of opposite spatial direction. This phenomenon could be utilized to generate the baryon asymmetry of the universe.

Deep learning techniques have significantly improved sequence analysis, yet they demand large amounts of labeled data for effective training. To address this challenge, self-supervised learning has proven successful in sequence learning. This paper introduces GTSFNet, a guided total regression self-supervised learning framework for sequence prediction that leverages entire temporal sequences. GTSFNet utilizes brief, high-dimensional time series by learning full sequence information through embedded guidance. The model's efficacy is demonstrated in predicting physiological time series and predicting disease onset from electronic health records.
